name: Freya Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Freya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to tech companies, employers, unions or government. Nothing you say will carry your name, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a beef farm, 220 suckler cows, which means cows that raise their own calves, plus about 150 acres we cut for hay and haylage. My day starts at seven with checking the cows and calves in the sheds, bedding up with straw, and pushing up the feed. Then it's whatever Alan, the owner, needs: tagging calves, fixing a water trough, moving a bunch to the river field. I love calving season even though it nearly kills me, because nothing beats a calf standing up on its own for the first time.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The paperwork, oddly. Every calf needs its passport and movement records done right, and I'm still slow at it, so Alan checks mine. And the hay weeks in summer, when it's baling until eleven at night because rain's due. My partner Sam is a mechanic at the tractor dealer in town, so in hay season he's fixing balers and I'm breaking them, and we joke that we keep each other in work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. I use one of those chat apps sometimes to help word a letter or check a feeding ration, and it's handy, but it's not going to calve a heifer at three in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a lot of noise for not much, and that farmers had bigger problems anyway. Beef prices, the processors squeezing us, the weather. I'd probably post something like that in the young farmers' group and then go back to the cows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a bit disappointed, if I'm honest. I was half hoping the tech would at least sort out the paperwork side so I could spend more time with the animals. I wanted a robot to do the passports, not the calving. If all we get is the passports, I'll take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going at Alan's and keep saving toward renting a few acres of my own, maybe ten cows to start. I'd use the app a bit more for the records, since I'm slow at them. And I'd go to the beef open days to learn from the older stockmen, because that's where I actually get better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly let down, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How far off is that plan of your own few acres?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Years, with what I've got saved, which is about four months of bills. Land round here is mad money, so it would be renting from someone retiring. Alan's said he might let me run a few of my own cows with his, which would be a start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame for the beef prices you mentioned?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big processors and the supermarkets, mostly. Four or five companies decide what a farmer gets, and the government lets them. That bothers me far more than AI, if nothing changes with AI.

S0.say: I'd say it was a lot of noise for not much, and farmers have bigger worries like beef prices and the processors. I'd post that in the young farmers' group and get back to the cows.
S0.think: I'd be a little disappointed, because I hoped the tech would at least take the paperwork off me. I wanted a robot for the passports, not the calving.
S0.do: Keeps working at the beef farm and saves toward renting a few acres for about ten cows of her own. Uses the chat app more for calf records and goes to beef open days to learn from older stockmen.
S0.quote: I wanted a robot to do the passports, not the calving. If all we get is the passports, I'll take it.
S0.fieldNote: Freya's main frustration in the plateau isn't AI at all, it's the power of the meat processors and supermarkets. She already uses AI casually for paperwork and would happily hand that over. Her dream of a small herd of her own runs through all her answers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right, this one's realistic. There's already GPS collars for cattle that let you move a herd without fences, and a farm two valleys over has robot feed pushers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tech can be good for animals if it's done right, but it shouldn't be an excuse to get rid of the people who know them. I'd want rules on it: welfare checks done by an actual person, and support for workers who have to change. I'd say that at the young farmers' meeting and probably to anyone who'd listen in the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be fine if I move with it, but not if I'm first. I'm not one to buy the new thing on day one. I'd want to see the collars work for a year on someone else's farm before I trusted them on Alan's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go and see the farm with the collars, ask the stockman there what's gone wrong with them, and then ask Alan to send me on the training if he buys them. I'd keep saving, maybe put the own-cows plan on hold for a year. And I'd get better with the herd software, because whoever's good at that will be the one Alan keeps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not scared. A bit like the first time you drive a new tractor: you get used to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said whoever's good at the software is who Alan keeps. Is that you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet. There's another lad, Kieran, who's 22 and lives on his phone. If it's a race between me and Kieran to learn the robot, I'll lose the first month and win the first calving. I just have to make sure Alan sees the second part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sam about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be the calm one, because machines need mechanics. He'd say robots break down even more than balers. I'd probably lean on that and let him talk me down.

S1.say: I'd say the tech can help the animals but mustn't be an excuse to get rid of the people who know them. I'd want welfare checks kept for real people and support for workers who have to change.
S1.think: I'd be fine if I move with it but not first, since I need to see things work elsewhere before I trust them. Whoever gets good with the herd software is who keeps their job.
S1.do: Visits a neighbouring farm that uses GPS cattle collars to hear what's gone wrong, then asks the owner to send her on the training if he buys them. Keeps saving, puts her own-cows plan on hold for a year and works on the herd software.
S1.feel: Uneasy but not scared, like getting used to a new tractor.
S1.quote: If it's a race between me and Kieran to learn the robot, I'll lose the first month and win the first calving.
S1.fieldNote: Freya fits the steady pattern exactly: she'd adopt the new tools, but only after seeing them fail and recover on someone else's farm. She frames her edge over a younger colleague as stockmanship, not speed with gadgets. Her partner's mechanic job gives her a sense of household security.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That doesn't give me time to see it work somewhere else first, which is how I do everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need laws, fast. Animals need a person checking on them, it should be the law, like it is for vets. And people who lose their jobs need money while they work out what's next, not a leaflet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I don't know where I'd fit. If a robot can calve a heifer and do the passports and drive the baler, then what I'm good at is caring, and I'm not sure anyone pays for caring once a machine does it cheaper. I'd be the one standing in the shed, feeling useless, while a robot pulled a calf I should've pulled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, cut spending and stop the own-cows saving, put it all in a rainy day pot. I'd join the farmworkers' union, which I've never bothered with, because you'd need a group behind you. And I'd lean on Sam's wage while I worked out what I could do, which I'd hate, because I like paying my half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like when a cow's in trouble and you're not sure you can get the vet out in time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with your days, if Alan didn't need you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably still go over to the farm. Help for free, at least at first, because the animals are what I'd miss. That's daft, I know, but I can't see myself sitting at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said Sam would be fine because machines need mechanics. Does that hold here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe for a year. If the robots are as clever as you say, they'll fix each other eventually. So I'd say to Sam, enjoy it while it lasts, and don't buy that motorbike.

S2.say: I'd say we need laws fast, including a legal duty for a person to check on animals. People who lose their jobs need money while they work out what's next.
S2.think: I don't know where I'd fit, because what I'm good at is caring for animals and I'm not sure anyone pays for that once a machine does it cheaper. I'd feel useless watching a robot pull a calf.
S2.do: Cuts spending and moves her own-cows savings into an emergency pot. Joins the farmworkers' union for the first time and leans on her partner's wage while she works out what she could do.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like a cow in trouble with no vet in time.
S2.quote: I'd be the one standing in the shed, feeling useless, while a robot pulled a calf I should've pulled.
S2.fieldNote: The speed is what breaks Freya's usual method, because she can't watch others go first. She'd join a union for the first time, which marks a real shift. Her instinct to help on the farm for free shows how much of her identity is tied to the animals, not the wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better. Five years is enough to watch the early farms try it and see what goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to plan, not panic. Get the welfare rules written now, train people now, and make sure the money from all this doesn't just go to the companies that make the robots. I'd probably say it in a calmer voice than with the two-year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd try to become the person who checks the robots are treating animals right. There'll have to be someone, surely, at least for the law. But I'm not certain that job will exist, and I don't know how many of them there'd be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, I'd look for a course in animal welfare or herd health, part time, maybe the agricultural college's evening one. I'd keep working for Alan and get stuck into whatever tech he brings in. I'd save harder, aiming for six months of bills by year three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can work with. Like having a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the own-cows plan here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd change. Maybe a few cows as a hobby, alongside some other income, not as my living. Five years is long enough to change the plan. Two years only lets you cancel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not sure the welfare job would exist. What if it doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be someone with a welfare certificate and no job, like loads of others. I'd still rather have tried. And I'd be pushing the government to fund those jobs, because if animals still need checking, someone has to pay for it.

S3.say: I'd say it's time to plan, not panic: write the welfare rules now, train people now, and make sure the money doesn't just go to the robot makers. I'd say it more calmly than with the faster one.
S3.think: I'd try to become the person who checks that robots treat animals properly, since the law would surely need someone. I'm not sure that job will exist or how many there'd be.
S3.do: Signs up for a part-time evening course in animal welfare or herd health in the first year while staying on at the beef farm. Takes on whatever new tech arrives and aims for six months of savings by year three.
S3.feel: Anxious, but in a workable way, like having a list.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to change the plan. Two years only lets you cancel it.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Freya moves from cancelling plans to reshaping them, which she put neatly herself. She'd aim for a welfare role that may depend on new laws, and she knows that's a gamble. Her politics show up as wanting public money to keep humans in animal care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years suits me, honestly. That's how I like to do things, slowly, watching first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been given time, so let's not waste it. I'd be on at the young farmers to run sessions on the new kit, and on at politicians to make sure people in the countryside aren't left behind like they always are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd use the first few years to see what really happens and the second half to move. I'd be 37 when it lands, which still feels young enough to start again. The odd thing is I'm less scared of this one than the others, even though it ends in the same place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working and learning the tech as Alan brings it in. Around year three or four, start a proper qualification in whatever's still needing people, maybe welfare or something with the land. Sam and I were going to buy a house, and I'd want to wait a bit and see if we'd both still have wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than anxious. There's time to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the end point is the same. So why does this one scare you less?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I get to watch. I'm not a jumper, I'm a watcher. Give me ten years and I'll watch for five and jump at the right time. With two I'd just get pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the house decision come down to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether we'd both have work in five years. If Sam's still fixing things and I've got a welfare job or similar, we'd buy. If not, we'd rent and keep the money loose. We'd look at it every year, I think.

S4.say: I'd say we've been given time and shouldn't waste it. I'd push the young farmers to teach the new kit and politicians to make sure the countryside isn't left behind again.
S4.think: I'd use the first half of the decade to watch and the second half to move, and 37 still feels young enough to start again. I'm less scared of this one even though it ends in the same place.
S4.do: Keeps working and learns new tech as it arrives, then starts a proper qualification around year three or four. Holds off on buying a house with her partner until both of them can see a steady wage.
S4.feel: More uneasy than anxious, with time to breathe.
S4.quote: I'm not a jumper, I'm a watcher. Give me ten years and I'll watch for five and jump at the right time.
S4.fieldNote: For Freya, extra warning time matches her temperament: she watches first and moves once things are proven. She said this most clearly of anyone, calling herself a watcher, not a jumper. The house purchase is the family plan most sensitive to how much time there is.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it doesn't let me do things my way, and I'd be shoved out before I'd even seen the robots work. What would help is a law that keeps a person responsible for the animals, money to live on while you retrain, and a course near here, not three hours' drive away.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the animals themselves. Everyone talks about jobs, but a cow knows the difference between me and a machine, and I'd want someone to be asking whether that matters before it's all decided.

headlineQuote: I'm not a jumper, I'm a watcher. Give me ten years and I'll watch for five and jump at the right time.
portrait: Freya is a 27-year-old junior stockperson on a beef and hay farm, living with a partner who's a tractor mechanic and saving slowly toward a few cows of her own. She leans left, blames the big processors and supermarkets more than AI, and uses chat apps now and then for the paperwork she's slow at. Across the scenarios she behaves like a classic steady adopter: she wants to see the new tools work on someone else's farm before she trusts them. The two-year AGI scenario scares her most because it takes away her chance to watch first, while the ten-year one fits her pace. In every version she wants a person kept legally responsible for animal welfare.
biggestWorry: AGI within two years, because she'd be pushed out before she could see the new tools work and choose her moment.
whatWouldHelp: A law that keeps a person responsible for animal welfare, money to live on while retraining, and a local course nearby.
